qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Define horizontal integration.
items.canonical_answer: Combining firms in the same industry at the same production stage.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Combining firms in the same industry at the same production stage.
objective_titles: Describe horizontal integration

items.prompt: Define forward vertical integration.
items.canonical_answer: Combining with a later production stage towards the final customer.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Combining with a later production stage towards the final customer.
objective_titles: Describe forward vertical integration

items.prompt: Define backward vertical integration.
items.canonical_answer: Combining with an earlier production stage supplying inputs.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): Combining with an earlier production stage supplying inputs.
objective_titles: Describe backward vertical integration

items.prompt: Identify the integration types when an invented tile manufacturer acquires its retailer and, separately, another tile manufacturer.
items.canonical_answer: The retailer acquisition is forward vertical; the other manufacturer acquisition is horizontal.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): later retailer is forward. Distinction/feature (1): same-stage manufacturer is horizontal.
objective_titles: Define and identify the different types of integration

items.prompt: Identify the integration type and its defining relationship in a tile manufacturer acquiring another tile manufacturer.
items.canonical_answer: Horizontal: both firms operate in the same industry at the same manufacturing stage.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): correct integration type. Characteristic/distinction with example (1): correct stage relationship from the original producer.
objective_titles: Describe horizontal integration

items.prompt: Identify the growth classification for an invented food processor taking ownership of the shop selling its output to households. Include the stage relationship from processing.
items.canonical_answer: Forward vertical integration: the acquired retail shop is downstream from processing, towards final customers.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): correct integration type. Characteristic/distinction with example (1): correct stage relationship from the original producer.
objective_titles: Describe forward vertical integration

items.prompt: Identify the integration type and its defining relationship in a tile manufacturer acquiring its clay supplier.
items.canonical_answer: Backward vertical: clay supply is an earlier input stage relative to the manufacturer.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): correct integration type. Characteristic/distinction with example (1): correct stage relationship from the original producer.
objective_titles: Describe backward vertical integration

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling a tile manufacturer’s acquisition of its clay supplier forward integration.
items.canonical_answer: It is backward vertical integration because the acquired activity supplies inputs at an earlier stage. Forward integration would move from manufacturing towards customers, such as acquiring a retailer.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): supplier direction mistaken for forward. Boundary/test (1): earlier input stage versus later retail stage.
objective_titles: Define and identify the different types of integration

items.prompt: Explain economies of scale using an original construction: plot output horizontally and long-run average cost in N$ per unit vertically for these invented output/cost points: 100/N$12, 200/N$9, 300/N$8. All inputs can be adjusted. Describe the pattern and an economic mechanism.
items.canonical_answer: Plot falling long-run average cost across the three points. Suitable technical specialisation or purchasing gains at larger scale can lower cost per unit; the schedule alone does not isolate the cause.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (2): output horizontally (1), long-run average cost N$/unit vertically (1). Initial position/original curve (1): first stated point. Change (2): remaining points correctly placed (1), falling/rising pattern identified (1). Explanation/interpretation (2): appropriate scale mechanism (1), long-run input-adjustment condition rather than fixed capacity (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Explain and illustrate the various economies of scale

items.prompt: Explain an invented large organisation’s diseconomies using a learner-constructed cost illustration. Its adjustable-input long-run alternatives are 300 units costing N$8 each, 400 costing N$9 each and 500 costing N$11 each. Construct labelled output/cost axes, mark these positions and interpret coordination delays as a possible cause of the rising section.
items.canonical_answer: Plot rising long-run average cost across the three points. Communication delays and coordination errors can add cost per unit as the organisation expands; this differs from adding workers to fixed equipment.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (2): output horizontally (1), long-run average cost N$/unit vertically (1). Initial position/original curve (1): first stated point. Change (2): remaining points correctly placed (1), falling/rising pattern identified (1). Explanation/interpretation (2): appropriate scale mechanism (1), long-run input-adjustment condition rather than fixed capacity (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Explain and illustrate the various diseconomies of scale

items.prompt: Analyse an invented long-run expansion from 100 units at N$12 average cost to 300 at N$8, where specialist equipment lowers unit cost and all inputs can adjust.
items.canonical_answer: Average cost falls N$4 per unit, illustrating technical economies of scale under the stated conditions. Total cost nevertheless rises N$1,200 to N$2,400, so the benefit is per unit rather than a smaller total bill.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): average cost falls. Evidence (1): N$12 to N$8. Explanation (2): technical scale gain (1), total cost can rise with volume (1).
objective_titles: Explain and illustrate the various economies of scale

items.prompt: Analyse a long-run expansion where output rises from 300 to 500 units and average cost from N$8 to N$11, with documented coordination delays and all inputs adjustable.
items.canonical_answer: Unit cost rises N$3, consistent with diseconomies of scale. Coordination delays add resources and rework per unit; the adjustable-input long-run case is different from diminishing returns to labour with fixed equipment.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): higher long-run unit cost. Evidence (1): N$8 to N$11. Explanation (2): coordination delays (1), distinct from fixed-input diminishing returns (1).
objective_titles: Explain and illustrate the various diseconomies of scale

items.prompt: Explain the confusion in calling a rise in long-run average cost as scale increases an economy of scale.
items.canonical_answer: A rise is a diseconomy of scale. An economy lowers long-run average cost; the direction of the unit-cost change distinguishes them.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): economies label applied to rising cost. Boundary/test (1): rising versus falling long-run average cost.
objective_titles: Explain and illustrate the various diseconomies of scale

items.prompt: Explain the net average-cost effect when expansion creates N$3 per unit technical/purchasing savings and N$1 extra coordination cost per unit, with other relevant costs unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: The N$1 diseconomy offsets part of the N$3 saving, leaving a net N$2 reduction in long-run average cost. The balance, rather than the existence of either effect alone, determines the direction.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): expansion brings both effects. Mechanism (2): N$3 saving (1), N$1 offset (1). Consequence (1): N$2 net unit-cost fall.
objective_titles: Discuss how the economies and diseconomies of scale affect business costs

items.prompt: Explain why a fall in average cost from N$12 at 100 units to N$8 at 300 does not mean a lower total cost.
items.canonical_answer: Despite economies of scale lowering the unit figure, total cost is average cost multiplied by output: N$1,200 initially and N$2,400 afterwards. Larger output can more than offset the lower per-unit amount.
marking_guidance: Context (1): multiply by corresponding output. Reason/conclusion (1): total doubles despite falling unit cost.
objective_titles: Discuss how the economies and diseconomies of scale affect business costs

items.prompt: Identify two distinct constraints on firm size, each with a brief example.
items.canonical_answer: A narrow market can leave large capacity without enough buyers. Limited finance can prevent purchase of the equipment required for expansion.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): market size and demand constraint. Distinct characteristic/example (1): capital availability and equipment constraint.
objective_titles: Discuss the main reasons for the different sizes of firms (size of market; capital; organisation), and the different factors that influence the size of a firm

items.prompt: Explain how this invented condition influences viable firm size: strong sustained orders.
items.canonical_answer: Confirmed saleable demand supports utilisation of larger capacity, making scale gains more feasible. A narrow or temporary market could leave that capacity idle.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): stated market, funding or organisational condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two relevant causal links from the facts. Consequence (1): larger scale supported or constrained, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain size of market through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why a customised tile firm with only a few stable monthly orders may remain small despite access to a larger machine.
items.canonical_answer: A larger machine does not create buyers. Limited saleable demand can leave it underused and make expansion unattractive.
marking_guidance: Context (1): relevant supplied constraint. Reason/consequence (1): explained link to feasible scale.
objective_titles: Explain size of market through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how this invented condition influences viable firm size: N$200,000 expansion cost but only N$60,000 available and no other funding.
items.canonical_answer: The N$140,000 funding gap prevents purchase of the proposed capacity, so market demand alone cannot make expansion feasible. Additional affordable funding or a smaller stage would be required.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): stated market, funding or organisational condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two relevant causal links from the facts. Consequence (1): larger scale supported or constrained, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain capital available through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the financing constraint where equipment requires N$200,000 but only N$60,000 is available and no additional funding is offered.
items.canonical_answer: The N$140,000 gap prevents this acquisition; expected demand does not itself supply the funds.
marking_guidance: Context (1): relevant supplied constraint. Reason/consequence (1): explained link to feasible scale.
objective_titles: Explain capital available through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how this invented condition influences viable firm size: several outlets without shared stock records, causing duplicated orders and delays.
items.canonical_answer: Expansion increases coordination demands. Missing shared records create errors and rework, adding cost per unit and limiting manageable size until organisation improves.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): stated market, funding or organisational condition. Because/mechanism (2): develop two relevant causal links from the facts. Consequence (1): larger scale supported or constrained, with its condition.
objective_titles: Explain organisation of the firm through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how clear responsibilities and a suitable shared stock record could ease growth problems caused by duplicated orders.
items.canonical_answer: They align decisions and information across outlets, reducing duplication and delay so the organisation can handle larger operations more effectively.
marking_guidance: Context (1): relevant supplied constraint. Reason/consequence (1): explained link to feasible scale.
objective_titles: Explain organisation of the firm through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Define horizontal integration (2). Identify the integration types for two acquisitions by a manufacturer: its retailer; its material supplier (2). Explain how specialist equipment can create an economy of scale where larger sustained output makes it economical (2). Identify two constraints on firm size (2).
items.canonical_answer: Horizontal integration combines firms in the same industry and stage. Retailer acquisition is forward and supplier acquisition backward vertical. Technical economies of scale from specialised equipment can lower long-run average cost when larger output supports its use. Market size and capital available can constrain scale.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): same industry (1), same stage combined (1). Separate points for identification (2): forward retailer (1), backward supplier (1). Explanation (2): specialist equipment used effectively at scale (1), lowers long-run average cost (1). Constraints (2): market (1), capital (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented expansion of Dune Tile Works: technical specialisation saves N$2 per unit and purchasing gains save N$1; coordination delays add N$1 per unit. These are all relevant long-run average-cost changes and quality is unchanged. A further expansion keeps the N$3 total savings but raises coordination additions to N$4. The first expansion has confirmed sustained demand and affordable funds; further expansion serves a narrow uncertain market and requires finance not yet offered. Describe three economies/diseconomies, each with its distinguishing case detail (6). Explain how these mechanisms affect unit costs at the two scales (7). Discuss whether further expansion is justified by cost and firm-size conditions (7).
items.canonical_answer: Technical specialisation saves N$2, purchasing N$1 and coordination adds N$1 initially. The savings total N$3; first expansion has a net N$2 average-cost fall, but at further scale N$4 coordination exceeds them and unit cost rises N$1. Further expansion is poorly supported: the unit-cost balance worsens, the market is narrow and finance is not secured. Potential gains remain, but changed organisation, sustained buyers and affordable funds would be needed to strengthen the case.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): technical economy (1), N$2 specialisation detail (1); purchasing economy (1), N$1 detail (1); coordination diseconomy (1), N$1 delay detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): specialisation improves resource use (1), purchasing lowers input cost (1), total saving N$3 (1); coordination consumes resources (1), first net fall N$2 (1), later coordination N$4 (1), later net rise N$1 (1). Both sides/judgement (7): potential scale savings (1), organisation might improve (1); net cost worsens (1), narrow market (1), unsecured capital condition (1); judgement further growth not justified now (1), tied to sales/funding/coordination constraints (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

facts: Invented expansion of Dune Tile Works: technical specialisation saves N$2 per unit and purchasing gains save N$1; coordination delays add N$1 per unit. These are all relevant long-run average-cost changes and quality is unchanged. A further expansion keeps the N$3 total savings but raises coordination additions to N$4. The first expansion has confirmed sustained demand and affordable funds; further expansion serves a narrow uncertain market and requires finance not yet offered.

items.prompt: Invented equal-quality expansion proposals. Case 1: a large stable market and affordable committed finance support larger scale; long-run unit savings N$3 exceed extra coordination costs N$1. Case 2: the market is narrow, finance is not secured, and N$3 unit savings face N$4 extra coordination costs. All relevant unit-cost changes are included. Evaluate expansion in Case 1 (7). Evaluate expansion in Case 2 (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: net unit cost falls N$2, sustained demand supports utilisation and affordable capital supports feasibility. Expansion is plausible while organisation and sales conditions hold, though lower unit cost alone does not measure total profit. Case 2: unit cost rises N$1, demand is narrow and capital is unsecured. Retaining a smaller scale is better supported until coordination, buyers and funding improve; potential technical savings alone do not settle the choice.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for net N$2 saving (1), stable market/capital support (1); argument against organisational risk (1), profit not established by unit cost alone (1); condition sustained utilisation and feasibility (1); judgement expand plausible (1), linked to balance and constraints (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for potential N$3 savings (1), organisation might be repaired (1); argument against net N$1 increase (1), narrow demand/unsecured finance (1); condition constraints addressed (1); judgement remain smaller for now (1), tied to current evidence (1). Total 14.
